---
title: "Quiz: moments as projections onto monomials"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Moments: $m_{pq} = \sum x^p y^q I(x, y)$; central moments $\mu_{pq}$ use $x - \bar x$, $y - \bar y$; $x$ to the right, $y$ down.

---

**Q1.** For a binary mask, $m_{00}$ is the area. What is $m_{00}$ of a grey image, and what is its centroid $(m_{10}/m_{00}, m_{01}/m_{00})$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The weight of every pixel is its grey value.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$m_{00}$ is the **total intensity** (the sum of all grey values). The centroid is the intensity-weighted mean position, the "centre of mass" if grey value is mass. It moves towards the bright parts.
:::

---

**Q2.** How many moments $m_{pq}$ are there with $p + q \le 3$? With $p + q \le 10$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Order $k$ has $k + 1$ moments: $(k, 0), (k-1, 1), \dots, (0, k)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10$ up to order 3. Up to order 10: $(N+1)(N+2)/2 = 11 \cdot 12/2 = 66$.
:::

---

**Q3.** A shape has $\mu_{30} = +115$ (per pixel of mass). You mirror it left–right. What happens to $\mu_{30}$, $\mu_{20}$ and $\mu_{21}$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Mirroring replaces $x - \bar x$ by $-(x - \bar x)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\mu_{pq}$ is multiplied by $(-1)^p$. $\mu_{30} \to -115$ (odd in $x$), $\mu_{20}$ unchanged (even), $\mu_{21}$ unchanged ($p = 2$ is even). The skewness along $x$ flips sign: the shape now leans the other way.
:::

---

**Q4.** A square and a disc have the same covariance matrix $S$. Which moment tells them apart first, and which shape has the larger value?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Both are symmetric under $x \to -x$: what does that do to every odd-order central moment?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
All odd orders are zero for both (point symmetric), order 2 is equal by assumption, so order 4 is the first difference. The kurtosis of the marginal is 1.8 for the square (flat, uniform) and 2.0 for the disc (a half-ellipse, more mass near the middle): the disc's is larger.
:::

---

**Q5.** Why should coordinates be mapped to $[-1, 1]$ before computing moments up to order 10?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How large is $x^{10}$ for $x = 255$, and how many significant digits does a double have?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$255^{10} \approx 1.2 \times 10^{24}$. A double carries about 16 significant digits, so in a sum of such terms everything below about $10^{8}$ is rounded away, and differences of large terms (central moments) lose most of their digits. In $[-1, 1]$ every weight is at most 1.
:::

---

**Q6.** A single pixel is counted as a point at its centre, or as a unit square. What is its $\mu_{20}$ in each case? What does the square model add to $\mu_{20}$ of an object of 548 pixels?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$\int_{-1/2}^{1/2} t^2\,dt$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
As a point: 0 (all mass at the centroid). As a square: $\int_{-1/2}^{1/2} t^2\,dt = 1/12 \approx 0.083$. Every pixel adds $1/12$, so the object's $\mu_{20}$ grows by $548/12 = 45.7$, i.e. $\mu_{20}/m_{00}$ by exactly $1/12$ (from 63.498 to 63.582 for the pear in the demo).
:::

---

**Q7.** The equivalent ellipse of an L-shaped object is tilted. Which order of moments first tells you in which corner the L has its "elbow"?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
An ellipse is point symmetric.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Order 3. Everything up to order 2 is the same for the L and its 180°-rotated copy (and for the ellipse); rotating by 180° flips the sign of every odd-order central moment. The signs of $\mu_{30}$, $\mu_{03}$, $\mu_{21}$, $\mu_{12}$ say on which side the extra mass lies.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* $F(u, v)$ is the Fourier transform of $f$. Which moment is $F(0, 0)$, and which is $\partial^2 F/\partial u^2$ at the origin?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Differentiate $e^{-2\pi i(ux + vy)}$ under the integral.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$F(0, 0) = \iint f = m_{00}$. $\partial^2 F/\partial u^2 = \iint (-2\pi i x)^2 f\, e^{\dots}$, at the origin $-4\pi^2 m_{20}$. Moments are the derivatives of the spectrum at zero frequency.
:::

---

**Q9.** Why can't five or ten moments in general reproduce an image exactly, even though *all* moments determine it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How many numbers does a $64 \times 64$ image have?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A $64 \times 64$ image has 4096 values; ten numbers cannot pin them down. In frequency terms: low-order moments fix the spectrum only near zero frequency, so fine detail (high frequencies) is not determined.
:::
